title: About
text:
This project combines historical and real-time financial data with AI to produce automated research reports for US growth stock investors. By feeding macroeconomic indicators, equity market data, and commodity prices into an AI model, each report identifies historical patterns, draws parallels to current conditions, and highlights risks and opportunities for growth-oriented portfolios.
All charts and visualizations in the reports are created by the author — the AI generates only the written analysis.

title: Market Research
text:
Geopolitical Shocks and Macro Crosscurrents: Navigating the Summer of 2026
Over the past three months leading up to July 24, 2026, global markets have been violently reordered by escalating geopolitical fractures, most notably the ongoing U.S. strikes on Iran and the Houthi blockade of the Red Sea, alongside intensified Russian missile offensives near Kyiv. These exogenous shocks have injected a severe risk premium into commodities, pushing Brent crude to $95.72 and gold to an unprecedented $4,067.60 by the end of July 2026, while the MSCI World Index has navigated the crosscurrents to close at 4,800.71. This environment of supply-chain disruptions, sticky inflation, and fragmented global trade bears a striking resemblance to the late 1970s and early 2000s market cycles, where geopolitical tail risks repeatedly tested equity valuations and forced a harsh repricing of long-duration assets.



MSCI World Equity Index


Looking domestically, the U.S. growth market is caught in a complex tug-of-war between resilient innovation and deteriorating macroeconomic foundations. The ongoing U.S. military engagement in the Middle East, with strikes continuing into their 13th night as the administration weighs a “massive response,” mirrors the supply-side vulnerabilities of the early 1970s. The resulting energy constraints have kept headline CPI sticky at 4.14% as of June 2026. In 1973, an oil embargo triggered an inflationary spiral that ultimately crushed the “Nifty Fifty” growth stocks of the era. Today, while CPI at 4.14% is nowhere near double digits, the mechanism—a geopolitical supply shock re-accelerating input costs and squeezing the consumer—is identical. For unprofitable or highly levered growth companies, a sustained Brent crude price near $100 acts as a hidden tax on future cash flows, compressing the very margins that justify today’s elevated multiples.



Brent Oil Prices


Investors are clearly pricing in a prolonged period of geopolitical instability, driving a historic flight to safety. Gold has eclipsed the $4,000 threshold, closing at $4,067.60 in July 2026, a level that signals deep institutional anxiety about fiat debasement and global trade fragmentation. This mirrors the late-stage 1970s when gold acted as the ultimate barometer for failing macroeconomic policies and runaway inflation expectations. When capital rotates aggressively into hard assets, it typically signals a lack of confidence in the real return of financial assets, creating a tough backdrop for high-multiple, unprofitable tech equities that rely on perpetual market optimism.



Gold Prices


Despite these macro headwinds, the equity indices have shown remarkable, albeit precarious, resilience. The S&P 500 sits at 7,436.52 and the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) at 28,322.76 as of July 2026. This stubbornness is partly fueled by tight credit markets; the BofA High Yield Option-Adjusted Spread is a mere 2.77% (July 2026), indicating that corporate debt rollover remains cheap and the “Zombie” company apocalypse has been temporarily staved off. Furthermore, the relentless pace of global innovation continues to provide a narrative floor, highlighted recently by the Fields Medal being awarded to Chinese mathematicians Hong Wang and Yu Deng for solving century-old problems—a reminder that the fundamental drivers of AI and algorithmic growth remain intact regardless of the macro weather.



Performance of Major US Stock Indices


However, the financial plumbing of the U.S. market resembles the late-stage liquidity squeeze of 1999, and the bond market is flashing historical warning signs. The Treasury market is demanding a higher term premium for long-duration risk. The 10-year yield stands at 4.562% while the 2-year yield is at 4.1933% as of July 2026, resulting in a positively sloped yield curve (a +0.36% spread). In early 2000, the yield curve steepened rapidly after a prolonged inversion, with the 10-year yield hovering around 6.0% to 6.7%. Today’s positive spread of +0.36% and 10-year yield at 4.562% mirrors the early stages of that yield curve steepening phase that preceded the dot-com crash. History warns us that when long-term yields refuse to capitulate despite a slowing economy (GDP growth fell to 2.1% in Q1 2026), the discount rate applied to next-decade earnings becomes a massive headwind for the NDX.



US 2Y and 10Y Treasury Yields and Spread


Compounding the yield pressure is the aggressive withdrawal of central bank liquidity. The Federal Reserve’s balance sheet has contracted significantly from its peak, settling at 6,737,644.25 million in July 2026. This quantitative tightening is draining the excess reserves that fueled the post-2020 tech boom. The combination of a shrinking Fed footprint and a stubborn 10-year yield is a toxic cocktail for growth stocks, echoing the 1999 liquidity crunch, where the marginal buyer of equities simply stepped out of the market.



Federal Reserve Total Assets


Yet, valuations remain stretched, demanding a high degree of perfection from corporate America. The S&P 500 trailing P/E ratio sits at 28.49 in July 2026. While not quite at the dizzying 30+ peaks of 2000, a 28.5x multiple leaves zero room for error in an environment where input costs are rising and the consumer is feeling the pinch of sticky 4.14% inflation and a 4.2% unemployment rate (June 2026). If earnings growth does not materially accelerate to justify these multiples, the market will rely entirely on multiple expansion—a feat nearly impossible to achieve when the 10-year yield is hovering near 4.6%.



S&P 500 PE Ratio


Based on these historical echoes and current market dynamics, here are the specific risks and opportunities for U.S. growth investors:

The Stagflationary Energy Shock (1970s Parallel): Escalation in the Middle East, particularly involving Iranian infrastructure or further Houthi disruptions, could push Brent crude past $120. This would re-accelerate CPI, forcing the Fed to halt or reverse its easing cycle, thereby devastating long-duration tech multiples that are currently priced for a soft landing.
Liquidity Drain & Yield Curve Steepening (1999 Parallel): If the 10-year yield breaches 5.0% due to term premium demands and Treasury supply issues, the historical correlation with NDX drawdowns suggests a severe multiple compression is imminent. The shrinking Fed balance sheet removes the natural bid for long-term bonds, leaving growth equities exposed to higher discount rates.
Defense-Tech and Cybersecurity Sovereignty: The Russian missile strike on a private training ground near Kyiv on July 24, 2026, and the U.S.-Iran conflict highlight the critical, inelastic need for modernized defense infrastructure. Growth companies in AI-driven defense, autonomous drone tech, and cybersecurity are seeing immediate government demand that is entirely decoupled from consumer cyclical risks and interest rate sensitivity.
Energy-Efficient & AI Infrastructure Optimization: High oil prices and sticky inflation favor B2B growth companies that actively reduce operational costs for other businesses. AI and cloud infrastructure platforms that optimize energy consumption, logistics, and supply-chain routing will command premium multiples as a necessary hedge against stagflationary pressures.

Suggested Portfolio Exposure for U.S. Growth Stocks: 25-50%
Justification: The current environment resembles a late-cycle transition where volatility is high, geopolitical tail risks are elevated, and broad market multiples are stretched against a backdrop of shrinking central bank liquidity. A 25-50% allocation allows for continued participation in secular, innovation-driven trends (like defense-tech and AI optimization) while preserving sufficient dry powder. If the 10-year yield breaches 5.0% or oil drives inflation back into the high 5s, triggering a growth correction, this cash reserve will be critical to redeploy into high-quality growth assets at more rational valuations.
